n: After burying the dead — so many that no one counted them — the surviving Nephites return home to their families.

f.w: the number of the slain were not numbered

n: The war’s cost reached far beyond soldiers: women and children were killed, livestock lost, and crops trampled by marching armies.
The enemy dead thrown into the river Sidon were carried away; Mormon says their bones lie in the depths of the sea.

f.w: cast into the waters of Sidon

n: Mormon pauses the war story to explain a detail: the Amlicites had painted red marks on their foreheads to identify with the Lamanites, though they did not shave their heads as Lamanite warriors did.

f.w: marked themselves with red in their foreheads
f.g: A self-chosen sign of allegiance, like war paint.

n: Lamanite warriors of this time shaved their heads and wore only loincloths of skin, along with their armor and weapons.

Mormon recounts the record’s explanation of the Lamanite “mark,” tying it to Laman and Lemuel’s rebellion against Nephi, Jacob, Joseph, and Sam. The Church today rejects any idea that skin color reflects God’s favor; the Book of Mormon itself teaches that all are alike unto God.

f.w: the mark which was set upon their fathers
Nephi, Jacob, and Joseph, and Sam

f.g: In the Book of Mormon the core “curse” is being cut off from the Lord’s presence (2 Nephi 5:20); it is lifted by repentance.

n: Because Laman, Lemuel, Ishmael’s sons, and their wives tried to kill their brothers, the Lord set a mark upon them, according to the Nephite record.

f.w: their brethren sought to destroy them

n: The stated purpose of the mark was separation — to keep the Nephites from adopting traditions that would lead them away from God. The concern in the text is belief and covenant, not ancestry.
Those who joined their lives with the Lamanites shared in their separation from the Nephite covenant community.

f.g: Intermarry; the issue throughout is allegiance and belief, as verse 11 makes clear.

n: Whoever chose to follow the Lamanites was counted as a Lamanite and shared their mark.

f.g: Classified under that name or group.

n: Mormon defines “Nephite” by faith rather than bloodline: anyone who believed the records from Jerusalem and kept God’s commandments was called a Nephite.

f.w: those records which were brought out of the land of Jerusalem

n: These faithful Nephites kept the true records of both peoples — the records Mormon is abridging.
Back to the Amlicites: they put a mark on themselves — red paint on their foreheads — by their own choice.

f.w: they set the mark upon themselves
f.g: Mormon’s point: their “mark” was self-inflicted, reflecting their own choice.

n: Mormon cites a promise to Nephi: the Lamanites would be marked and separated unless they repented and turned to God for mercy. The door to mercy was always open.

f.w: except they repent of their wickedness and turn to me

n: He quotes another part of the promise: those who joined the Lamanites would share the same mark.

f.w: I will set a mark upon him
f.g: This saying is not preserved in Nephi’s small plates; Mormon may be quoting the large plates.

n: And: whoever fights against Nephi’s people would bear a mark.
Those who leave the Nephite faith lose the name of Nephi’s seed, while those who are counted as his seed receive the Lord’s blessing — again a matter of choice and covenant.

f.w: he that departeth from thee shall no more be called thy seed

n: The Amlicites didn’t realize they were fulfilling prophecy when they marked their foreheads. Having openly rebelled against God, they brought the consequences on themselves.
Mormon’s lesson: people bring curses and condemnation upon themselves by their own choices. God does not arbitrarily condemn anyone.

f.w: bring upon himself his own condemnation

n: Soon after the first battle, another Lamanite army invades at the same spot.

f.g: The Nephites have little time to recover.

n: An army is sent to drive the invaders out.

f.w: drive them out of their land
f.g: Nephite wars in this book are generally defensive.

n: Alma, wounded in the earlier battle, does not lead this time.
Alma sends a large army that defeats the Lamanites and pushes them out of Nephite borders.

f.w: out of the borders of their land
f.g: Securing the frontier rather than conquering new territory.

n: The army returns home, and the land enjoys peace for a while.

f.g: Peace in the book of Alma is often short-lived.

n: All these wars began and ended within the fifth year of the judges — a single terrible year.
Mormon reflects soberly: in one year tens of thousands entered the next life to receive the reward of the spirit they chose to follow — good or evil.
Each person receives “wages” from whomever he chooses to obey. Our choices determine our master and our reward. So ends the fifth year.

f.w: every man receiveth wages of him whom he listeth to obey
